title: California Insurance Code Section 10110.1 (insurable interest in life and disability insurance, including an employer's interest)
claims: Section 10110.1(a) defines an insurable interest, with reference to life and disability insurance, as an interest based upon a reasonable expectation of pecuniary advantage through the continued life, health, or bodily safety of another person and consequent loss by reason of that person's death or disability, or a substantial interest engendered by love and affection in the case of individuals closely related by blood or law.

Section 10110.1(b) provides that an individual has an unlimited insurable interest in his or her own life, health, and bodily safety and may have a policy on his or her own life made payable to whomsoever he or she pleases, regardless of whether the beneficiary has an insurable interest.

Section 10110.1(c) provides that, except as provided in Section 10110.4, an employer has an insurable interest in the life or physical or mental ability of any of its directors, officers, or employees, or those of any of its subsidiaries, or any other person whose death or physical or mental disability might cause financial loss to the employer.

Section 10110.1(c) provides that an employer has an insurable interest, pursuant to any contractual arrangement with any shareholder concerning the reacquisition of shares owned by the shareholder at the time of his or her death or disability, in the life or physical or mental ability of that shareholder for the purpose of carrying out the contractual arrangement.

Section 10110.1(c) provides that an employer has an insurable interest, pursuant to any contract obligating the employer as part of compensation arrangements or as guarantor or surety, in the life of the principal obligor.
Section 10110.1(c) provides that the employer shall obtain the written consent of the individual being insured.

Section 10110.1(c) provides that the trustee of an employer, or of a pension, welfare benefit plan, or trust established by an employer providing benefits to employees and retired employees and acting in a fiduciary capacity, has an insurable interest in the lives of the employees and retired employees for whom those benefits are to be provided.

Section 10110.1(d) provides that trusts and special purpose entities used to apply for and initiate the issuance of policies for investors, where one or more beneficiaries do not have an insurable interest in the life of the insured, violate the insurable interest laws and the prohibition against wagering on life, and section 10110.1(e) provides that any device, scheme, or artifice designed to give the appearance of an insurable interest where there is no legitimate insurable interest violates the insurable interest laws.

Section 10110.1(f) provides that an insurable interest shall be required to exist at the time the contract of life or disability insurance becomes effective, but need not exist at the time the loss occurs.

Section 10110.1(g) provides that any contract of life or disability insurance procured or caused to be procured upon another individual is void unless the person applying for the insurance has an insurable interest in the individual insured at the time of the application.

Section 10110.1(h) provides that, notwithstanding subdivisions (a), (f), and (g), a charitable organization that meets the requirements of Section 214 or 23701d of the Revenue and Taxation Code may effectuate life or disability insurance on an insured who consents to the issuance of that insurance.
Section 10110.1(i) provides that the section shall not be interpreted to define all instances in which an insurable interest exists.
Section 10110.1 was last amended by Stats. 2009, Ch. 343, Sec. 1 (SB 98), effective January 1, 2010.
notes: The employer's insurable interest in subdivision (c) opens with an exception: except as provided in Section 10110.4, which restricts corporate-owned life insurance on non-exempt California employees. Subdivision (c) also carries its own written consent requirement, which is a California requirement separate from the federal notice and consent in 26 U.S.C. 101(j)(4).
